name: Grace Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a small housing charity, the kind that helps people who are about to lose their flat. I get in at half eight, check the voicemail, and book tenants in with our four caseworkers. Then it's filing: tenancy forms, benefit letters, notes from home visits, all scanned and put in the right folder. I'm still learning the case system, to be honest, and I mess up the folder names more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tenants. A woman came in last week with every letter from her landlord in a carrier bag, and sorting them into date order calmed her right down. What wears me out is the phone. It rings forty times a day, and half of it is people who are scared and angry, and I'm the first voice they hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly. At work I'd tell the caseworkers we can stop worrying about being replaced and get back to fighting for funding. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into social housing instead of chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change my real problem, which is that our main grant runs out in March. If the council doesn't renew it, the office shrinks, and the junior admin goes first. That's me. So AI flopping is nice, but I'm still checking the job sites on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd carry on using the AI thing now and then to tidy up letters, because it does save me ten minutes. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, and I'd go to the union branch meeting about the grant cuts. Jonah, my partner, says I should ask my manager straight out what happens in March, so maybe I'd finally do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but with the same knot in my stomach I've had since the summer. The knot isn't about robots. It's about one funding letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the junior admin goes first. Has anyone actually told you that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody's said it, but I watched it happen at my last job at a dentist's. They cut the newest person and gave her work to the receptionist who'd been there ten years. I'm the newest person here, and I still mislabel files, so I know where I sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the grant isn't renewed, what's the first thing that changes at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the weekend away we're saving for, that's first. Jonah's wage covers the rent but not much more, so my pay is the food and the bills. We've got about three months of my wages saved, which feels like a lot until you picture actually using it.

say: I'd call it **good news** for office workers and tell colleagues to focus on the **funding fight** instead.
I'd post that the money should have gone into **social housing**, not chatbots.
think: My real threat is the **grant renewal** in March, not AI.
If the office shrinks, the **newest admin** goes first, and that's me.
I'm still **mislabelling files**, so I don't feel safe on skill either.
do: Keep using the AI tool **now and then** to tidy letters and save ten minutes.
Go to the **union branch** meeting about grant cuts this autumn.
Ask my manager **straight out** what happens to my job in March.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, but the same **knot** about funding stays.
S0.quote: We've got about three months of my wages saved, which feels like a lot until you picture actually using it.
fieldNote: Her worry is **funding**, not technology, and AI Plateau barely touches it.
She reads her own position through a **past layoff** she watched at a dentist's.
Household relies on her pay for **food and bills**, so even a mild world feels shaky.

steps.text: Ask my manager what happens to my job if the March grant ends
Go to the union branch meeting on grant cuts
Put a set amount aside each month toward a fourth month of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the charity should use it to free us up for tenants, not to cut staff. I'd say it loudly at the union meeting too, because this is exactly where you need rules on how bosses bring it in. Online I'd share stuff about councils using it to deny people help, because that already scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, booking, filing, chasing letters, that's my whole job, and that's the list on your card. If our trustees can buy software that books the caseworkers and files the forms, they'll take it, because they're always short of money. I don't think I'd be sacked on day one, but I think they wouldn't replace me when I left, and they'd stop giving me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just now and then, because I'd rather be the one who knows how the new booking system works. I'd ask our manager if I can sit in on the caseworkers' calls, because helping tenants face to face feels harder to hand to software. And I'd look at the evening housing advice course at the college, it's two nights a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not hopeless. There's time in this one, and I'm not bad at picking things up once I've seen someone else do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be the one who knows the new system. Isn't that helping it replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. If the booking software comes anyway, I'd rather be the person who trains everyone on it than the person it gets rid of. My mum always says you don't stop the bus by standing in front of it, you get on and argue with the driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doreen, our part-time bookkeeper, honestly. She's sixty-one and does everything on paper, and if invoices go automatic she's gone. She taught me how the filing works when I started, so it'd feel awful to be learning the thing that pushes her out.

say: I'd argue the charity should use AI to **free up time** for tenants, not cut staff.
I'd push the **union** for rules on how managers bring the software in.
think: Booking and filing are **my whole job**, and they're on the list AI takes.
I'd lose **hours** and not be replaced, rather than get sacked outright.
do: Learn the **new booking system** properly so I train others on it.
Ask to **sit in** on caseworker calls to move toward face-to-face work.
Sign up for the **evening course** in housing advice, two nights a week.
feel: **Anxious** but not hopeless, because there's **time** to adjust.
S1.quote: If the booking software comes anyway, I'd rather be the person who trains everyone on it than the person it gets rid of.
fieldNote: She sees her own duties listed on the card and names the **hours cut** as the likely path.
Steady adapter: she'd learn the tool once it's **proven**, and frames it as self-defence.
Real guilt toward **Doreen**, the older bookkeeper, shows a strong sense of fairness.

steps.text: Learn the charity's new booking software well enough to train others
Take the college's two-night housing advice course
Raise rules on staff cuts at the union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down, and that governments need to step in now. I'd be posting about a basic income, because if every desk job goes in two years there's no other answer. At work I'd say we need a plan for the tenants, because they'll be hit worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done as an office administrator by 2028. My job is screens and paper and the phone, all thinking work, so nothing about it waits for the robots. I'm twenty-seven with no degree, and I'd be up against every other admin, receptionist and call-centre worker for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go after hands-on work, because your card says robots don't come till 2031, so that's three years. I'd look at care work or training as a support worker at the hostel we refer people to. I'd stop all the extras and push our savings from three months to five if I can, and I'd go to every union meeting, because this needs people standing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. I keep picturing the empty desk with a tablet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of hands-on work, and then the robots come too. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd be hoping by then that governments had sorted something out, a basic income or a jobs guarantee. I'm not going to pretend I've got a plan for 2031, I'd just be trying to get there with some money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his job's safer than mine for now, because buses still need someone with spanners. Then I'd tell him we need to stop talking about getting a bigger flat. He'd say it'll be fine, and I'd want to believe him.

say: I'd demand **government action** now and post in favour of a **basic income**.
At work I'd say we need a plan for **tenants**, who'll be hit worst.
think: I'm finished as an **office administrator** by 2028, because nothing in my job waits for robots.
With **no degree**, I'd be competing with every admin and receptionist.
do: Apply for **care or support work** at the hostel within months.
Stop extras and grow savings from **three to five months**.
Attend every **union meeting** on job losses.
feel: **Scared**, picturing an empty desk with a tablet on it.
S2.quote: My job is screens and paper and the phone, all thinking work, so nothing about it waits for the robots.
fieldNote: She grasps that her work is **all thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help her.
Her escape route is **hands-on care**, which only buys about three years.
She openly has **no plan** for 2031 and hopes government acts by then.

steps.text: Apply for a support worker post at the partner hostel
Stop extras and build savings from three to five months
Attend every union meeting about job losses
Drop plans for a bigger flat this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but I'd be sounding it louder because there's actually time to do something. I'd say the unions and the government have five years, so no excuses. I'd be the annoying one sharing petitions in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about how long it'd take me to become someone with a real skill. That's what it means to me. I've got just enough time to turn into something other than the junior who mislabels the files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the support worker qualification part-time next year while keeping the admin job, so the pay keeps coming. I'd use the AI tools more at work in the meantime, because if I'm still there in 2029 I want to be the one running them. And I'd save harder, maybe four months by 2030, because the care pay is lower at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care pay is lower. Can you and Jonah live on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, if we stay in this flat. We'd have to forget the car, and the holiday in Portugal we keep promising ourselves would turn into a weekend at his parents'. That's fine, I'd rather be broke and working than comfortable and out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come for care work in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think people will still want a human in the room when they've just been evicted or their mum's dying. Maybe I'm kidding myself. But I'd rather bet on that than on filing.

say: I'd say unions and government have **five years** and no excuses.
I'd share **petitions** in every group chat about protecting workers.
think: Five years is just enough to become someone with a **real skill**.
My best bet is that people want a **human in the room** at hard moments.
do: Start a **support worker qualification** part-time next year while keeping my job.
Use **AI tools** more at work to run the new systems.
Save toward **four months** by 2030, since care pay starts lower.
feel: **Nervous**, but it feels like a race she **could run**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be broke and working than comfortable and out of a job.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her fear into a **training plan** she can name.
She accepts a **pay drop** and fewer comforts to stay in work.
Her hope rests on a belief that **human presence** matters in crises.

steps.text: Start a part-time support worker qualification next year
Run the new AI booking tools at the charity until 2029
Save toward four months of bills by 2030
Share union petitions on protecting office workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd want the union pushing for paid retraining now, not in 2035. Online I'd be the one saying this is a policy choice, not the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which sounds old to me now but isn't. I can make a whole career change in ten years, I just have to actually start, and I'm not great at starting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in admin for a couple of years and learn the AI tools as they come in, because that pays the rent. Around year two I'd start the support work training, and by year five I'd want to be doing it full-time. We'd also think properly about whether to have kids, because I'd want my job sorted first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. A bit restless, like a long to-do list I haven't begun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not great at starting things. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably someone signing me up. If the union or the charity said, here's a paid course, Tuesday nights, it's booked, I'd go. If it's left to me, I'll still be saying next year in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this change your plans with Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around thirty. In this one I'd push that back to thirty-two or so, so I'm settled in the new job first. He'll grumble, but he's patient.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** and push the union for **paid retraining** now.
I'd keep saying online that this is a **policy choice**, not bad weather.
think: At thirty-seven I can make a **full career change**, if I start in time.
My real risk is **not starting**, because I put things off.
do: Stay in **admin** for two years and learn the AI tools as they arrive.
Begin **support work training** around year two, full-time by year five.
Push back plans for **children** until the new job is settled.
feel: **Calmer**, but **restless**, like a to-do list not yet begun.
S4.quote: If the union or the charity said, here's a paid course, Tuesday nights, it's booked, I'd go. If it's left to me, I'll still be saying next year in 2033.
fieldNote: Her job still disappears, so the change is **control**, not safety.
She admits **procrastination** is her real risk and wants a nudge from outside.
Family plans move: **children** pushed back until the new career is settled.

steps.text: Learn each new AI tool at the charity for two years
Enrol in support work training around the second year
Push back having children until about age thirty-two
Press the union for paid retraining courses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, by a mile. My whole job goes and I've got no degree and three months of savings. What would help is a paid course I'm put on, not one I have to find myself, and the union fighting for some kind of income floor while we retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the people around us matter. I keep thinking about Doreen, our bookkeeper, and the tenants, not just me. If this goes badly, the people we help at the charity get hit twice, once by losing work and once by losing the people who used to help them.

headlineQuote: If this goes badly, the people we help at the charity get hit twice, once by losing work and once by losing the people who used to help them.
portrait: Grace is a **junior administrator** at a small housing charity, booking caseworkers and filing tenancy papers.
She's **progressive** and a union member, and sees AI as a question of **fairness** and policy.
Her deepest worry already exists: a **grant renewal** in March that could cut her post.
She adapts once a path is clear, picking **care and support work** as her way out.
She admits she **puts things off** and would thrive if someone booked the course for her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her whole job is thinking work and she has no degree.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** she's signed up to, plus union pressure for an **income floor** during retraining.
